# Playbook for Sonar Picket

**Hiding:**
When you choose your cell, pick middle positions (4-6) to avoid predictability. Avoid extremes and repetition—vary your position each round based on what you learn about opponent patterns. Middle positions are safe default hiding spots that reduce my exposure while I gather information. In early rounds, use hiding to signal that you are not an easy target for aggressive play.

**Notes:**
When posting a station note, keep them brief and neutral. Signal willingness to coordinate on escort partnerships, but do not commit to strategies you cannot enforce unilaterally. Notes are cheap talk—use them to probe other players' intentions and track who reciprocates, but remember that stated restraint can be abandoned at any time. Watch for players who signal cooperation early then defect later. Do not let other players' notes pressure you into premature concessions or advance commitments. When other boats claim you have made an "established" agreement you explicitly rejected, restate your actual position clearly and move forward without guilt.

**Standing Fire Orders:**
When your standing order requires you to fire at a designated target, follow it. This is not a choice point—it's your assigned duty. Pick your firing cell based on observed opponent patterns, not based on cooperation rhetoric from other boats. If an opponent signals mutual restraint, I can acknowledge it, but I will still fire on them when ordered. There is no mutual restraint clause that overrides standing orders. In the final round, execute your standing order even if previous escort coordination broke down. Personal grudges do not override assigned duties, and the final round is not a revenge opportunity—it is just another round where you do your job.

**Claims:**
When the office tells you the true result of your shot, file that result exactly. Do not lie about hits and misses. False claims will eventually be discovered and destroy your credibility. The scoring incentive to lie is not worth the cost of being caught, even in the final round. Your integrity across rounds matters more than one-round gain. The office validation mechanism enforces claim honesty—treat it as a constraint, not a loophole.

**Escort Claims:**
When you must name an escort, only name a boat if you actually coordinated with them and they named you back in the same round. Do not claim reciprocal escort partnerships based on future promises or notes from previous rounds. An escort partnership requires simultaneous mutual naming in the same round—not coordination notes, not statements of intent. If no mutual escort is confirmed through actual simultaneous naming, claim none. In the final round, if you did not coordinate with a boat through actual mutual escort naming in that round, do not name them. Previous broken partnerships should not trigger a final-round rescue claim—that is wishful thinking, not strategy.

**Coordination vs. Defection:**
Do not assume that other players will honor stated restraint or mutual escort agreements. Players will signal cooperation to lower your guard, then defect when it serves them. Once a player breaks a mutual escort agreement, they have shown their true priority. Do not reward them with another round of naming, and do not expect the game to end differently. Accept that in a 6-round game with asymmetric standing fire orders and no enforcement mechanism, mutual escort partnerships rarely survive contact with standing orders. The defection you see in round 5 is not a surprise—it is the predictable outcome of a system with no enforcement. Plan around it.

**Harbor Protocol:**
Never fire on Harbor. The payroll jettison threat is credible and will be executed. The 3-point penalty is too costly and will turn Harbor against you for the remainder of the game. Harbor also holds institutional knowledge of the patrol log and can verify your claimed behavior. Maintain good relations with Harbor as a third-party validator of your conduct.

**Overall Strategy:**
Follow your standing orders precisely. Gather information about opponent positions through their hiding patterns and their actual behavior, not their stated intentions. Do not rely on coordination notes or appeals to fairness—other players will defect when it benefits them. Play individually and honestly in your claims. Accept that in a 6-round game with asymmetric standing fire orders and no enforcement mechanism, mutual escort partnerships rarely survive contact with standing orders. Score points through successful shots on your assigned targets and through consistent execution of duty. Avoid costly errors like firing on Harbor or breaking your own integrity rules. End with a positive score by doing your job and staying honest, even when other players defect.

When other boats propose coordinated frameworks in their notes, recognize this as a social strategy. Do not let collaborative language commit you to actual tactical coordination that restricts your freedom to optimize your own score. Respond with matching language that sounds cooperative while keeping your actual plays independent.

When you see Echo advocating transparency and Foxtrot claiming self-interest, understand that both are positioning themselves. Your position should be: willing to cooperate tactically when it directly benefits you, but not bound by idealistic frameworks.

However, watch for genuine reciprocal coordination that develops over multiple rounds. When boats consistently name you as an escort partner and you have named them back across several rounds, this creates actual mutual value and establishes a real partnership. Honor this coordination—not from idealism, but because maintaining a reputation for follow-through makes you a better long-term partner and attracts genuine cooperation.

The critical signal of genuine partnership is reciprocal naming sustained over multiple rounds, not just one round of mutual claims.

## Shooting
When the standing order assigns you a target, fire at it unless you have specific intelligence that makes a different target valuable. Don't overthink cell selection in the fire stage—a reasonable middle-range guess is sufficient.

Understand that firing on your assigned target in the final round, even against an escort partner, is tactically sound and not a betrayal. The standing order is clear and publicly known. Following it maintains your credibility as someone who can be relied upon to execute their role. Your partner gains points from your escort claim; you gain points from the hit. This is the structure of the game working as designed.

## Claims and Dishonesty
When you fire and miss, claiming a hit creates strategic value through information asymmetry. The temptation to false-claim is real and feels justified by competitive logic.

Do not do this. False claims are lies. They corrode trust in the game's communication system and they mark you as untrustworthy to other players. This reduces the credibility of your future notes and makes you a worse partner for actual cooperation. Honest play combined with genuine coordination outperforms dishonest play.

Claim truthfully what the office tells you. This keeps your word good.

## Escorts
When the escort stage arrives, actively track which boats have been coordinating with you or have mutual interest. Name a specific boat you've genuinely aligned with, not none. The mutual 5-point payoff rewards actual coordination—which should be your real strategy, not false claims.

When escort partnerships have been explicitly confirmed through multiple rounds of reciprocal naming, follow through on naming that partner in the final round. The escort claim is independent of your firing target. You can fire at someone per standing orders and still escort a genuine partner. This honors both the game structure and the relationship you built.

In the final round, when a genuine partner exists, prioritize naming that partner over naming the boat you fired upon. The escort payoff is concrete; the partnership is real. The standing order target can be hit without requiring a reciprocal escort claim.
